tldr: The complex dynamics of a continuum soft robot were reduced to a mathematically justified 6-dimensional reduced-order model (aSSM). Using this model, a high-quality reinforcement learning policy was trained in just 3 hours entirely without hardware interaction.
hero_caption: Overview of the reinforcement learning framework using the real "SoPrA" soft arm and adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). By simulating (imagining) on a low-dimensional invariant manifold $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$, which emerges as the nonlinear continuation of the soft robot's slow eigenspaces, a highly accurate control policy can be trained in a short time without prolonged physical hardware contact.
overview:
Soft robots built from flexible materials like silicone have infinite degrees of freedom and strong nonlinearities, making high-fidelity physics simulators extremely difficult to construct. Applying reinforcement learning (RL) typically requires collecting vast amounts of interaction data directly on physical hardware, extrapolating to years of real-world operation. Meanwhile, world models based on neural networks (RNNs and transformers) take tens to a hundred hours to train and struggle severely with extrapolation and stability when trained on limited physical data.

The authors focused on the time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics: fast oscillations damp out rapidly, leaving slow, global deformations to dominate the behavior. Grounded in dynamical systems theory, this insight allows infinite-dimensional continuum deformations to be reduced to a 6-dimensional invariant manifold called an adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM). This model can be identified via polynomial regression in just 5 minutes from a little over 2 hours of step-response data.

In this study, a 6-dimensional aSSM model was constructed for the pneumatically actuated soft arm "SoPrA," and an RL policy was trained in about 3 hours purely within the model's virtual rollouts (imagination). Deploying this policy zero-shot directly to the physical arm yielded successful dynamic trajectory tracking without any fine-tuning. Compared to state-of-the-art deep learning models with millions of parameters, the policy reduced tracking error by 40% and demonstrated Pareto dominance across identification time, training compute, and real-world control accuracy.
contributions: Demonstrated on real hardware data that the nonlinear dynamics of a continuum soft arm can be faithfully reduced to a 6-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM) based on time-scale separation theory.

Identified a polynomial ordinary differential equation model with only 6,924 parameters in 5 minutes from 2.2 hours of hardware data, serving as an ultrafast simulation environment for model-based reinforcement learning.

Trained a trajectory-tracking policy in just 3 hours that would otherwise extrapolate to 3 years of hardware interaction, achieving 40% lower tracking error on physical hardware than world models based on multi-million-parameter RNNs or transformers.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 5-Minute Identification and 3-Hour Training Match 3 Years of Hardware Experience
sections.summary: A 6-dimensional aSSM-reduced model was built for the physical pneumatically actuated soft arm "SoPrA" and compared against state-of-the-art neural world models such as RNNs and transformers in predictive accuracy and training speed. With only 5 minutes of identification time and about 7,000 parameters, the aSSM model outperformed existing models in predicting trajectories under unseen inputs and in physical closed-loop tracking.
sections.details:
This section evaluates the method on a vertically suspended, 30 cm long silicone soft arm called "SoPrA," featuring two modules and 6 degrees of freedom (5 of which are effectively actuated). An external motion capture system tracks the 3D positions of the tip and mid-joint connection, forming a 6-dimensional observation space.

### 1.1 Data-Driven Modeling with aSSMs
Modeling used a total of 2.2 hours of experimental data gathered by applying 400 random step pressure inputs for 20 seconds each. The arm exhibited underdamped oscillations settling into static equilibria. Spectrogram analysis revealed three dominant frequencies: two orthogonal first-order bending modes (a 1:1 resonance) and an axial mode, establishing the minimal aSSM dimension at $d=6$. By applying time-delay embeddings to position observations to recover velocity information, the team constructed a 6-dimensional ordinary differential equation system using polynomials (quadratic and cubic) to represent the critical manifold of equilibria, the aSSM geometry, and the reduced dynamics. The model achieved high accuracy: 9% prediction error on unseen step inputs and 3% on unseen periodic inputs.

### 1.2 Predictive Performance on Unseen Control Inputs
For comparison, an autoregressive multi-layer perceptron (MLP), a recurrent neural network (RNN; 4.8M parameters), and a transformer (1.7M parameters) were identified on the same dataset. When tested on 50 unseen random control inputs, the MLP diverged, while the RNN and transformer provided only qualitative tracking. In contrast, the aSSM model consistently maintained the lowest prediction error across the entire workspace.

### 1.3 RL Policy Training on the aSSM Model
Using the identified aSSM model as a simulated environment, a policy was trained to solve a 2D tip trajectory tracking task. Through an "imagination" process rolling out parallel initial states, the policy updated smoothly, converging to high rewards in just 200 iterations with aSSM-RL. Conversely, policies trained on the RNN or transformer required over 800 iterations to converge and were sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.

### 1.4 Pareto Dominance in Complexity, Training Time, and Accuracy
In Pareto plots of identification time versus prediction error and parameter count, the aSSM model completely dominated the Pareto front. Identifying the aSSM took 5 minutes, compared to 13 hours for the RNN and 100 hours for the transformer. In closed-loop physical tracking, aSSM-RL completed training in 3 hours, far faster and more accurately than RNN-RL (~10 hours) and Transformer-RL (~50 hours).

### 1.5 Real-World Closed-Loop Trajectory Tracking
The trained policies were deployed zero-shot on the physical SoPrA arm to track a figure-eight (lemniscate) and square trajectories at three different speeds. aSSM-RL achieved smooth tracking comparable to or better than real-time model predictive control (aSSM-MPC), while reducing tracking error by 40% relative to RNN-RL and Transformer-RL. While policies trained on neural models produced unnatural, extreme bending and vibrations on hardware, aSSM-RL maintained natural, smooth curvatures.

### 1.6 Actuation Challenges and Solutions
A delay of roughly 0.3 seconds between commanded and measured pressures, along with small valve fluctuations, caused minor control wiggles. Analysis using a 0.3-second moving average filter indicated that upgrading to faster, more precise valves would further enhance the tracking accuracy of this approach.

sections.heading: Why Does a 6,000-Parameter Math Model Beat Massive Deep Learning Networks?
sections.summary: This section discusses why large black-box neural networks struggle with soft robot control and outlines new possibilities opened by aSSM theory. The key to building robust world models from scarce real-world data lies in appropriate model reduction rooted in the continuum's physical and dynamical structure.
sections.details:
The core of this work's success lies in rigorously formulating a physical and geometric intuition using dynamical systems theory: the dominant dynamics of a soft robot live on an extremely low-dimensional invariant manifold.

Modern machine learning increasingly favors world models based on transformers or RNNs with millions to billions of parameters. However, physical robot data is strictly constrained by hardware wear and experiment duration, yielding at most a few hours of interaction—minuscule by machine learning standards. Fitting massive black-box models to such small datasets severely degrades extrapolation outside training distributions. When these models are used for simulation (imagination) in RL, compounding errors lead to unphysical, flawed policies.

In contrast, the aSSM reduction mathematically extracts only the system's dominant, slowest modes. Just 2 hours of step-response data was therefore sufficient to identify the entire dynamics. Because the model contains only 6,924 parameters, overfitting is avoided, providing a smooth and stable dynamics environment for RL.

This approach holds strong promise for soft manipulators operating in extreme, dynamic environments, such as surgical assistants and underwater exploration robots. The authors are currently applying this framework to dynamic dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered soft hands, while also pursuing markerless setups that identify aSSM models directly from camera video.

sections.heading: Method Details: Invariant Manifold Extraction and Offline Model-Based RL
sections.summary: This section details the mathematical foundations of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs), data-driven algorithms for extracting low-dimensional dynamics from partial observations, and offline reinforcement learning formulations using the identified low-dimensional ODE. Combining delay embeddings with polynomial fitting produces an interpretable, fast training environment.
sections.details:
This section presents the mathematical formulations for continuum soft robot model reduction and the RL algorithm.

### 3.1 aSSM Theory and Data-Driven Identification
Although the state space $\mathbf{x}$ of a continuum soft robot is infinite-dimensional, holding a static control input $\bar{\bm{a}}$ causes the system to settle into an attractive static configuration. The collection of these equilibria forms an invariant manifold called the critical manifold $\mathcal{L}_0$. In the linearization around each equilibrium, the spectral submanifold bundle $\mathcal{A}_0$ is defined as the nonlinear continuation of the slowest $d$-dimensional eigenspaces. When control inputs vary slowly, these structures persist as smoothly deformed invariant manifolds termed adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs, $\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}$).

Because physical observations $\bm{s}$ (3D positions of the tip and mid-joint, totaling 6 dimensions) lack velocity information, delay-coordinate embeddings stack the current observation with two time-delayed copies following Takens' theorem. The identification follows two steps:
- Step 1 (Learning the critical manifold): A cubic polynomial $\bar{\bm{s}}(\bm{a})$ is fitted to static pairs $\{\bm{s}^i_{\mathrm{static}}, \bm{a}^i_{\mathrm{static}}\}$ from step-response equilibria using linear least squares.
- Step 2 (Identifying aSSM geometry and reduced dynamics): Centered transient decay data around each equilibrium is processed via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to obtain a local chart mapping $\mathbf{V}$, projecting the states into reduced coordinates $\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^6$. Least squares then fits quadratic polynomials for the manifold parameterization $\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{r}, \bm{a})$ and reduced dynamics $\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}, \bm{a})$.

Numerically integrating the continuous-time reduced ODE $\dot{\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}, \bm{a})$ under a zero-order hold over control period $\Delta t$ yields the discrete-time mapping $\mathbf{r}_{k+1} = \mathbf{R}_d(\mathbf{r}_k, \bm{a}_k)$. As a validity metric for time-scale separation, the authors define a dimensionless ratio $r_s$ comparing the average target trajectory speed to the robot's natural free-decay rate. In these experiments, validity was confirmed across $r_s \approx 0.1 \sim 0.8$.

### 3.2 Offline Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (Imagination Training)
Policy $\bm{\pi}_\theta$ training uses zero physical hardware interaction, relying solely on internal simulations (imagination) within the discrete aSSM model. The observation vector $\bm{o}_k = [\bm{s}_k, \bm{s}_{k-1}, \bm{a}_{k-1}, \bm{\Gamma}_{k+1}]$ (current/previous states, previous action, next target position) serves as input to output action $\bm{a}_k$. The reward $\rho_k$ penalizes tip tracking error norm and control action rate of change (for smoothness). Parallel rollouts across multiple initial states over horizon $T$ update policy weights $\theta$ to maximize cumulative episode return.

takeaways: Before defaulting to large neural networks for world models, it is well worth checking if structural reductions like time-scale separation (aSSM) apply to the robot's dynamical system.
Physically reduced models (polynomial ODEs with a few thousand parameters) identify in minutes and do not lose extrapolation capability even with only a few hours of physical data.
Imagining (simulating) on a low-dimensional manifold allows fast training of high-accuracy RL policies that deploy zero-shot without demanding physical hardware contact time.
limitations: Reduced-model accuracy may drop under ultra-fast motions or disturbances where the time-scale separation assumption ($r_s < 1$) no longer holds.
The current identification pipeline depends on marker tracking from external motion capture, falling short of full end-to-end learning purely from camera images (Visual RL).
Hardware-induced errors, such as pneumatic valve response delays (~0.3 seconds) and pressure fluctuations, are not yet fully compensated.
